items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the way people are spread out across an area”.
items.answer: Population distribution
items.markingKey: Population distribution: the way people are spread out across an area. [1]

items.stem: Explain why some areas of the world are sparsely populated, using two examples.
items.answer: Extreme climates (Sahara too hot and dry, Antarctica and northern Canada too cold), high mountains (Himalayas) with steep slopes and thin soils, and dense forests (Amazon) make farming, building and transport difficult.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason with example up to [4]

items.stem: Explain why river valleys and deltas are often densely populated.
items.answer: Flat land and fertile alluvial soils are good for farming; rivers provide water and transport; e.g. the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta and the Nile valley.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each factor; 1 mark example [3]

items.stem: The table shows population and area for three regions of a country. Northern District: population 120 000  area 4 000 km². Capital Region: population 1 000 000  area 500 km². River Delta: population 1 080 000  area 1 200 km². Suggest two reasons why Northern District is sparsely populated.
items.answer: Cold climate or poor soils, few jobs and remoteness from the capital.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason [2]

items.stem: The table shows population and area for three regions of a country. Coastal Plain: population 125 000  area 500 km². Northern District: population 75 000  area 2 500 km². Capital Region: population 8 750 000  area 2 500 km². (a) Identify the most densely and most sparsely populated regions. (b) Suggest two reasons why Northern District is sparsely populated.
items.answer: (a) Most dense: Capital Region (3500 per km²); most sparse: Northern District (30 per km²). (b) Cold climate or poor soils, few jobs and remoteness from the capital.
items.markingKey: (a) densities calculated for all three [2] (b) 1 mark each reason [2]

items.stem: “Physical factors are more important than human factors in explaining population distribution.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: climate and relief; water and soils; technology.
items.answer: Agree: Most people live where climate, relief, soil and water allow farming: river valleys, coastal plains. Deserts, mountains and polar areas remain almost empty. Disagree: Human factors such as jobs, trade, transport and government decisions explain the growth of cities in difficult places (Dubai, Singapore). In high-income countries people live where jobs and services are. Judgement: Physical factors explain the broad global pattern; human factors explain patterns at a local scale and in more developed economies.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: A student writes: “Large countries always have the largest populations.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Russia and Canada are huge but sparsely populated, while Bangladesh is small but has about 170 million people.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the number of live births per 1000 people per year”.
items.answer: Birth rate
items.markingKey: Birth rate: the number of live births per 1000 people per year. [1]

items.stem: Country D has a birth rate of 18 per 1000 and a death rate of 6 per 1000. Suggest which stage of the Demographic Transition Model the country is in, and explain your choice.

items.stem: Country C has a birth rate of 14 per 1000 and a death rate of 8 per 1000. (a) Suggest which stage of the Demographic Transition Model the country is in, and explain your choice. (b) Describe the shape of population pyramid you would expect for this country.
items.answer: (a) Stage 4: low birth and death rates, so little growth. (b) Narrow base, wide middle and top: an ageing population.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark stage; 1 mark use of both rates [2] (b) 1 mark shape; 1 mark link to rates [2]

items.stem: Country A has a birth rate of 45 per 1000 and a death rate of 7 per 1000. (a) Use the “rule of 70” (doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate %) to estimate how long the population would take to double. (b) Describe the shape of population pyramid you would expect for this country.
items.answer: (a) about 18 years (b) Wide base narrowing quickly with age (triangular): many children, few elderly.
items.markingKey: (a) 70 ÷ 3.8 [2] (b) 1 mark shape; 1 mark link to rates [2]

items.stem: “An ageing population causes more problems than a youthful population.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: migration; jobs and education.
items.answer: Agree: Rising pension and health costs fall on a shrinking workforce (e.g. Japan). Labour shortages may slow economic growth. Disagree: Youthful populations (e.g. Niger) need many schools, jobs and health services and can lead to unemployment. Older people contribute through volunteering, childcare and spending. Ageing countries can attract migrant workers and use technology. Judgement: Both create challenges; youthful populations are often harder for poorer countries to manage, while ageing is a bigger issue for richer countries.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the increase in the proportion of a country’s population living in towns and cities”.
items.answer: Urbanisation
items.markingKey: Urbanisation: the increase in the proportion of a country’s population living in towns and cities. [1]

items.stem: Explain why the number of megacities has increased since 1950.
items.answer: Rapid rural-urban migration in lower- and middle-income countries for jobs and services, combined with natural increase as young migrants have children; industrial growth and globalisation have concentrated jobs in large cities.
items.markingKey: 1 mark migration; 1 mark natural increase; 1 mark economic growth [3]

items.stem: Explain the difference between urbanisation in high-income and lower-income countries.
items.answer: In HICs urbanisation happened mostly in the 19th and early 20th centuries and is now slow, with suburbanisation and counter-urbanisation; in LICs and NEEs it is happening rapidly now, driven by migration and natural increase.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each; 1 mark contrast [3]

items.stem: In 1980, Country K had a population of 40 million, of whom 20% lived in urban areas. By 2020 its population was 80 million and 45% lived in urban areas. Explain why urban population grew faster than total population.
items.answer: Rural-urban migration moved people from the countryside to cities, in addition to natural increase in both areas, so the urban share rose.
items.markingKey: 1 mark migration; 1 mark share rises [2]

items.stem: In 1980, Country K had a population of 20 million, of whom 20% lived in urban areas. By 2020 its population was 40 million and 55% lived in urban areas. (a) Calculate the urban population in 1980 and in 2020. (b) Calculate how many times larger the urban population became.
items.answer: (a) 4 million and 22 million (b) 5.5 times

items.stem: How far do you agree that the growth of megacities brings more benefits than problems? Use your own knowledge to support your answer. You may wish to consider: inequality; jobs and wealth; housing.
items.answer: Agree: Megacities concentrate jobs, investment, universities and services and produce a large share of national wealth (e.g. Mumbai). Disagree: Rapid growth leads to informal settlements, congestion, pollution and pressure on water and sanitation (e.g. Lagos, Dhaka). Inequality between rich and poor is often extreme. Judgement: Megacities offer major opportunities, but benefits outweigh problems only where growth is well planned and managed.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: In 1970, Country K had a population of 40 million, of whom 20% lived in urban areas. By 2020 its population was 80 million and 45% lived in urban areas. How many people lived in urban areas in 2020?
items.answer: 36 million
items.markingKey: 45% of 80 million = 36 million. [1]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “an area of unplanned housing built by residents on land they do not legally own, usually lacking basic services (a slum or shanty town)”.
items.answer: Informal settlement
items.markingKey: Informal settlement: an area of unplanned housing built by residents on land they do not legally own, usually lacking basic services (a slum or shanty town). [1]

items.stem: Explain why informal settlements develop in rapidly growing cities.
items.answer: Migrants arrive faster than formal housing can be built; they cannot afford rent or land; they build homes on unused land such as hillsides, river banks and near railways, close to work.
items.markingKey: 1 mark rapid migration; 1 mark cannot afford formal housing; 1 mark location [3]

items.stem: Explain two problems faced by people living in informal settlements.
items.answer: Lack of clean water and sanitation spreads diseases such as cholera and diarrhoea; overcrowding and fire risk; no legal ownership, so homes can be demolished; risk of floods and landslides; insecure informal jobs.
items.markingKey: 2 marks each explained problem [4]

items.stem: Explain why population density figures for a whole country can be misleading.
items.answer: They are averages that hide uneven distribution: e.g. Egypt’s average density is moderate, but about 95% of people live along the Nile and in its delta, while most of the country is empty desert.
items.markingKey: 1 mark averages hide variation; 1 mark example [2]

items.stem: Explain why death rates fall in stage 2 of the Demographic Transition Model.
items.answer: Improvements in medical care, vaccinations, clean water, sanitation and food supply reduce deaths, especially of infants and children.

items.stem: A population pyramid shows that 25% of a country’s people are aged 0-14, 46% are aged 15-64 and 29% are aged 65 and over. (a) Calculate the dependency ratio. (b) Explain why the dependency ratio is only an approximate measure.
items.answer: (a) 117.4 (b) Many people over 65 still work and many aged 15-19 are in education, not working; some children work; it ignores unemployment.

items.stem: Evaluate the view that the Demographic Transition Model is a useful way to understand population change in all countries. You may wish to consider: government policy; disease; European experience.
items.answer: Agree: It describes the experience of many countries, such as the UK, well. It helps predict future changes in birth and death rates. Disagree: It was based on European experience; some countries moved through stages much faster or got “stuck”. It ignores migration and government policies (e.g. China’s one-child policy). Diseases such as HIV/AIDS raised death rates in some countries. Judgement: It is a useful general model but needs adapting for individual countries.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: What is meant by the term “migration”?
options: Money sent home by migrants to their families.
A person who has left their country and asked for protection as a refugee in another country, but whose claim has not yet been decided.
The movement of people from one place to another to live, either permanently or for a long period.
The country to which migrants move.
items.answer: The movement of people from one place to another to live, either permanently or for a long period.
items.markingKey: Migration: the movement of people from one place to another to live, either permanently or for a long period. [1]

items.stem: Explain two positive impacts of immigration on a host country.
items.answer: Fills labour shortages (e.g. health care, construction, farming); migrants pay taxes and spend money; cultural diversity in food, music and ideas; young migrants balance an ageing population.
items.markingKey: 2 marks each explained impact [4]

items.answer: Benefits refugees bring, or why they fled Syria.

items.stem: How far do you agree that migration brings more benefits than problems to host countries? Use your own knowledge to support your answer. You may wish to consider: public services; culture and identity.
items.answer: Agree: Migrants fill labour shortages, pay taxes and start businesses. They add cultural diversity and help balance ageing populations. Disagree: Rapid immigration can put pressure on housing, schools and health services in some areas. Tensions and discrimination can arise; some migrant workers are exploited. Judgement: Overall the economic benefits are usually greater, though they depend on how well governments plan for and support migrants.

items.stem: Explain two opportunities that living in a megacity can offer.
items.answer: More jobs (formal and informal) and higher wages; access to schools, universities and hospitals; better transport and internet; cultural and social opportunities.

items.stem: A student writes: “Informal settlements are places where nobody works.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many residents work in the informal economy or formal jobs nearby; Dharavi has thousands of small businesses.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Case study: Dharavi, an informal settlement in Mumbai, India, home to about 1 million people in roughly 2 km². Many residents work in recycling, leather, pottery and garment workshops. Describe two challenges for people living in this settlement.
items.answer: Lack of clean water and toilets, open drains and disease; overcrowding and fire risk; insecure land rights and risk of eviction; flooding or landslides.

items.answer: Jobs, investment and technology can overcome physical problems: e.g. Dubai and Las Vegas have grown in deserts using desalination, air-conditioning and trade or tourism jobs.

items.answer: Steep slopes, thin soils and a colder climate make farming and building difficult; poor transport.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason [2]

items.stem: “Population density tells us more than total population about the pressure on a country’s resources.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: demand for resources; uneven distribution.
items.answer: Agree: Density shows how crowded land is, e.g. Bangladesh and Singapore compared with Australia or Canada. Disagree: Density is an average that hides uneven distribution (e.g. Egypt along the Nile). Resources, technology and wealth matter: Singapore is very dense but wealthy, while some sparsely populated areas struggle. Total population shows overall demand for food, energy and jobs. Judgement: Density is helpful, but pressure on resources depends on how people are distributed and how resources are used.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the birth rate minus the death rate, when births are greater than deaths”.
items.answer: Natural increase
items.markingKey: Natural increase: the birth rate minus the death rate, when births are greater than deaths. [1]

items.stem: Explain what a population pyramid with a “bulge” in the 20-34 age group might show.
items.answer: In-migration of young adult workers (e.g. to cities or Gulf states), or a past baby boom.
items.markingKey: 1 mark migration; 1 mark alternative explanation [2]

items.stem: A population pyramid shows that 42% of a country’s people are aged 0-14, 38% are aged 15-64 and 20% are aged 65 and over. Suggest two consequences of this dependency ratio for the government.
items.answer: Must fund pensions, health and social care for older people with fewer taxpayers; may encourage immigration or raise the retirement age.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Country D has a birth rate of 26 per 1000 and a death rate of 11 per 1000. (a) Use the “rule of 70” (doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate %) to estimate how long the population would take to double. (b) Describe the shape of population pyramid you would expect for this country.
items.answer: (a) about 47 years (b) Base starting to narrow, wider middle.
items.markingKey: (a) 70 ÷ 1.5 [2] (b) 1 mark shape; 1 mark link to rates [2]

items.stem: “An ageing population causes more problems than a youthful population.” How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. You may wish to consider: level of development; jobs and education.
items.answer: Agree: Rising pension and health costs fall on a shrinking workforce (e.g. Japan). Labour shortages may slow economic growth. Disagree: Youthful populations (e.g. Niger) need many schools, jobs and health services and can lead to unemployment. Older people contribute through volunteering, childcare and spending. Ageing countries can attract migrant workers and use technology. Judgement: Both create challenges; youthful populations are often harder for poorer countries to manage, while ageing is a bigger issue for richer countries.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: What is meant by the term “push factor”?
options: Movement of people within the same country, such as from rural to urban areas.
A person forced to leave their country because of war, persecution or violence, protected under the 1951 Refugee Convention.
The movement of people from one place to another to live, either permanently or for a long period.
A reason that makes people want to leave a place, such as unemployment, conflict or drought.
items.answer: A reason that makes people want to leave a place, such as unemployment, conflict or drought.
items.markingKey: Push factor: a reason that makes people want to leave a place, such as unemployment, conflict or drought. [1]

items.stem: Explain two negative impacts of emigration on a source country.
items.answer: Loss of young, skilled workers (brain drain), e.g. doctors and nurses; an ageing population left behind; families separated; farms and businesses short of labour.
items.markingKey: 2 marks each explained impact [4]

items.stem: Country N has a GDP of about US$36 billion. Remittances from about 3 million citizens working abroad are equal to 15% of GDP. Suggest one risk of an economy depending heavily on remittances.
items.answer: If the host countries’ economies decline (e.g. a fall in oil prices or a pandemic), remittances fall suddenly; it can discourage investment in local jobs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark risk; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: How far do you agree that the source country loses more than it gains from emigration? Use your own knowledge to support your answer. You may wish to consider: brain drain; remittances.
items.answer: Agree: Brain drain removes doctors, nurses and teachers; rural areas lose young workers; families are separated. Disagree: Remittances raise incomes and pay for schools and health care (e.g. Nepal). Returning migrants bring skills and savings. Emigration reduces unemployment. Judgement: It depends on who leaves: losing skilled professionals is damaging, but remittances from labour migration can bring large benefits.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: “Migration brings more benefits than problems to host countries.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion.
items.answer: Agree: Migrants fill labour shortages, pay taxes and start businesses. They add cultural diversity and help balance ageing populations. Disagree: Rapid immigration can put pressure on housing, schools and health services in some areas. Tensions and discrimination can arise; some migrant workers are exploited. Judgement: Overall the economic benefits are usually greater, though they depend on how well governments plan for and support migrants.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Most of the world’s megacities are now in Asia, Africa and Latin America.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Examples include Delhi, Shanghai, Dhaka, Cairo, São Paulo, Mexico City, Mumbai and Lagos.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why young adults are the group most likely to migrate to cities. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Most of the world’s megacities are now in Asia, Africa and Latin America.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) They are looking for work and education, have fewer family responsibilities and are more willing to take risks; their move also increases cities’ birth rates. (b) Correct. Examples include Delhi, Shanghai, Dhaka, Cairo, São Paulo, Mexico City, Mumbai and Lagos.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reason; 1 mark development [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: In 1960, Country K had a population of 60 million, of whom 15% lived in urban areas. By 2020 its population was 120 million and 40% lived in urban areas. Explain why urban population grew faster than total population.
items.answer: Rural-urban migration moved people from the countryside to cities, in addition to natural increase in both areas, so the urban share rose.
items.markingKey: 1 mark migration; 1 mark share rises [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Giving residents legal ownership of their homes can encourage them to improve them.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. With secure tenure, people are more willing to invest in better building materials and services.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Read Source A carefully. “Narrow lanes are lined with workshops where people recycle plastic, tan leather and make pottery. Up to 1500 people may share one public toilet, and the open drains overflow during the monsoon.” (A magazine article about Dharavi, Mumbai, written in 2020 (adapted).) Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of living conditions in an informal settlement that Source A does not show.
items.answer: How residents view their community, or plans to redevelop Dharavi.
items.markingKey: 1 mark accurate own knowledge; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: Case study: Kibera, an informal settlement in Nairobi, Kenya, home to hundreds of thousands of people near the city centre. Many residents work in small shops, tailoring, charcoal and recycling. (a) Describe two challenges for people living in this settlement. (b) A district has a density of 80 000 people per km². Calculate how many people would live in 0.5 km² at this density.
items.answer: (a) Lack of clean water and toilets, open drains and disease; overcrowding and fire risk; insecure land rights and risk of eviction; flooding or landslides. (b) 40 000 people
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each challenge [2] (b) 80000 × 0.5 [1]
